answer: STRENGTHS: (1) Real, well-articulated pain point: small cities lack affordable, consistent vacancy data, and grant programs increasingly require data-backed need. (2) Clear niche focus (small/mid-sized cities, vacancy only, simple UX, low price) that avoids head-on competition with large platforms. (3) Working prototype plus informal validation: demoed to two city offices and a regional planning group with positive feedback. (4) Complementary, credible team: planning domain knowledge (Marcus, with municipal office exposure), statistics/modeling (Priya), and engineering (Tobias). (5) Low burn and capital-light structure; LLC registered, small spend, so downside is limited. (6) Founders are self-aware about gaps (sales, data access, privacy, market sizing) and ask for targeted help. (7) Dual-signal approach (utility + mail status) is conceptually sound and gives a defensible accuracy story if validated. WEAKNESSES: (1) Data access is the existential risk: utility data usually sits behind utility-company agreements, regulatory constraints, and privacy rules; no agreements exist, and USPS-style delivery-status data is partly restricted/licensed. The core product depends on inputs not yet secured. (2) No paying customers, no signed pilots, no letters of intent; 'useful' feedback is weak evidence of willingness to pay. (3) Unvalidated accuracy: no reported ground-truth testing of the scoring model (precision/recall vs field surveys), which is critical for credibility with planners and grant reviewers. (4) Market sizing is vague ('several hundred cities', 'low thousands of dollars') and implies a small revenue ceiling (roughly low single-digit millions at best), more lifestyle/small business than venture scale. (5) Government sales are slow, budget-constrained, and procurement-heavy; the team has no sales or public-sector selling experience and a 3 to 5 pilot target in a year may be optimistic for conversion to paid. (6) Weak defensibility: signals are 'not unique in principle', incumbents (data vendors, planning software) can add vacancy features, and the moat rests mainly on speed and relationships. (7) Part-time student founders with unclear commitment, no financial model or detailed unit economics, and a recurring-data-acquisition cost structure that may compress margins. (8) Privacy/legal exposure (utility usage data, property-level inference about occupancy) is acknowledged but unaddressed. OVERALL: Interesting, credible early-stage idea with a genuine need and a capable founding team, but investment interest is moderate-to-low (roughly 4/10): too early, dependent on unresolved data access, unproven demand and accuracy, and limited scale. It merits mentorship and small grant-style support to run pilots, not significant equity investment until data agreements, validated accuracy, and paid pilots exist.
